title: Validating short-term PROgnostic models for LONG-term outcomes in early severe mental disorders
summary:
Early mental health conditions such as psychotic disorders and depression can follow very different trajectories. Individuals at clinical high risk (CHR) for psychosis also show highly diverse long-term outcomes. While some people recover well, others experience persistent symptoms or long-term difficulties in everyday functioning.
Previous studies, including the Personalized Prognostic Tools for Early Psychosis Management (PRONIA) study and the Cannabis-Induced Psychosis (CIP) study, developed prediction models that use clinical and other characteristics to estimate disease trajectories over several years.
The aim of the present study is to reassess individuals who participated in the PRONIA or CIP studies 7 to 12 years ago. The study will evaluate how well these previously developed prediction models can forecast long-term clinical and functional outcomes. In addition, factors that may influence the course of illness will be examined, including life events, social support, substance use, and changes in symptoms and behaviour in everyday life. To this end, participants will complete interviews and questionnaires and take part in several months of smartphone-based monitoring.
The findings will contribute to a better understanding of the long-term course of mental health conditions and may help improve the prediction of individual outcomes in the future.
